name: Coinbase

summary.text: Coinbase is a U.S. cryptocurrency exchange led by chief executive Brian Armstrong. FactCheck.org identifies it as one of the three largest contributors to the crypto super PAC Fairshake, alongside Ripple Labs and Andreessen Horowitz. It gave Fairshake $25 million in June 2024 and in October 2024 announced a further $25 million for the 2026 midterms. Armstrong has said the company's aim is to elect pro-crypto candidates of both parties and vote anti-crypto candidates out of office.

facts.claim: In early June 2024 Coinbase gave $25 million to the Fairshake super PAC, days after President Biden vetoed a congressional resolution on crypto custody accounting; Ripple and Andreessen Horowitz had each given $25 million in late May 2024.

facts.claim: Brian Armstrong wrote in 2024 that 'The best way to get regulatory clarity in democratic countries is to elect pro-crypto candidates on both sides of the aisle, and to vote anti-crypto candidates out of office,' in explaining Coinbase's $25 million support for Fairshake.

facts.claim: On October 30, 2024 Armstrong announced on X that Coinbase would give Fairshake a further $25 million in 2025 for the 2026 midterms, saying the next Congress 'will be the most pro-crypto' yet and 'we're not slowing down'. On November 4, 2024 Fairshake said it had raised $78 million for 2026 including new commitments from Coinbase and Andreessen Horowitz.

facts.claim: On June 6, 2023 the SEC filed a complaint against Coinbase, Inc. and Coinbase Global, Inc. in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York (No. 1:23-cv-04738). The SEC alleged that Coinbase operated its crypto asset trading platform as an unregistered national securities exchange, broker and clearing agency, and that it failed to register the offer and sale of its staking-as-a-service program; it sought injunctive relief, disgorgement and civil penalties. Coinbase said in its quarterly report that it disputed the claims and intended to defend against them. A complaint is an allegation.
facts.quote: The Securities and Exchange Commission charged Coinbase, Inc. with operating its crypto asset trading platform as an unregistered national securities exchange, broker, and clearing agency.

facts.claim: On March 27, 2024 Judge Katherine Polk Failla denied most of Coinbase's motion for judgment on the pleadings. She found that the SEC had sufficiently pleaded that Coinbase operates as an unregistered exchange, broker and clearing agency and adequately alleged that its staking program involved the unregistered offer and sale of securities, and she rejected Coinbase's 'major questions doctrine' and fair-notice arguments. She dismissed the SEC's claim that Coinbase acted as an unregistered broker through its self-custody Wallet app. The ruling was on the pleadings and was not a finding that Coinbase violated the law.
facts.quote: The court finds that the SEC adequately alleges that Coinbase, through its Staking Program, engaged in the unregistered offer and sale of securities

facts.claim: Judge Failla later granted Coinbase's motion for an interlocutory appeal, sending the question of whether the Howey test applies to the crypto asset transactions at issue to the Second Circuit and pausing the SEC's case; she wrote that conflicting decisions on the issue necessitated the Second Circuit's guidance.

facts.claim: On February 27, 2025 the SEC announced that it had filed a joint stipulation with Coinbase, Inc. and Coinbase Global, Inc. to dismiss its pending enforcement action against both companies with prejudice. The SEC said the dismissal rested on its judgment that ending the case would facilitate its ongoing efforts to reform its approach to the crypto industry, not on any assessment of the merits of the claims, and that the decision did not reflect its position on any other case.

facts.claim: In statements on the February 27, 2025 dismissal of the Coinbase case, Acting Chairman Mark Uyeda said the agency's views on crypto had largely been expressed through enforcement actions without engaging the general public; Commissioner Hester Peirce said she had not supported the action against Coinbase; and Commissioner Caroline Crenshaw dissented, calling the move unprecedented and saying it ignored the court's earlier finding that the Commission had adequately pleaded violations of the securities laws.

facts.claim: On February 21, 2025 Coinbase chief legal officer Paul Grewal wrote on the company's blog that SEC staff had agreed in principle to dismiss the case pending commissioner approval, that Coinbase had always maintained it was right on the facts and the law, and that the dismissal was 'a victory not just for Coinbase, but for our customers, the United States, and individual freedom'. Brian Armstrong called the news 'hugely vindicating' and said the company would not pay any fine.

openQuestions: Basic company facts (founding year, Nasdaq listing in 2021) were not sourced in this run.

Coinbase's total giving to Fairshake differs by source and period: more than $75 million (NBC/CNBC, 2024 cycle, in fairshake.json), about $93.5 million (Bloomberg Government analysis of FEC data as cited by Wikipedia, 2023-2024), and $52.46 million for the 2026 cycle (Wikipedia). Fortune reported Coinbase had also given more than $20 million in 2023. None of these was verified at the FEC.
The Armstrong 'regulatory clarity' quote was attributed in search results to a 2024 blog post; the Fox Business article is cited as the carrier. The owner should confirm the original post.
Reports that Armstrong personally gave $1 million to Fairshake and that a 2025 gift was $24.5 million from Coinbase plus $1 million from Armstrong came from aggregator sites and are not recorded.

The SEC's February 27, 2025 release and Coinbase's FY2025 Form 10-K differ by a day on the stipulation of dismissal (February 27 versus February 28, 2025); whether and when Judge Failla so-ordered it was not checked on the docket.

The date of Judge Failla's order granting Coinbase's interlocutory appeal to the Second Circuit was not captured (The Block's report is undated in the record here; reported elsewhere as January 2025). The status of that appeal before the February 2025 dismissal was not checked.
Commissioner Peirce's and Commissioner Crenshaw's February 27, 2025 statements are cited for their characterisations of the dismissal; the full text of the SEC release was not read.
